body_markdown:
BMW’s Motorsport division never got its hands on the original, E53-generation X5, so an enthusiast commissioned a restomod that explores what a first-generation X5 M could have looked like. Unveiled during Monterey Car Week, this BMW X5 V-10 is a one-off that features M5 power, a six-speed manual transmission, and all-wheel-drive in addition to numerous custom styling cues inside and out.


Built for Ronnie Fieg, the founder of New York City-based fashion brand Kith, the E53 was treated to a full restoration before the swap began. This makes it one of the first E53s to get a complete restoration, though it likely won’t be the last: The model made its debut in 1999 and[it’s approaching classic status](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/is-the-bmw-x5-on-its-way-to-collector-status/) . Fieg’s example was entirely taken apart and repainted in Titanium Silver Metallic.


Visually, we spot a handful of styling cues that denote there’s serious power under the hood. The X5 features a redesigned front bumper inspired by the one fitted to the V-12-powered X5 Le Mans prototype, new side skirts, and a specific rear bumper with four exhaust outlets. Inside, there’s a 175-mph speedometer and Kith-branded upholstery on the seats, among other modifications.

The real treat is under the hood. The restoration shop stuffed a 5.0-liter S85 V-10 borrowed from the E60-generation M5 in the engine bay. It’s linked to a six-speed manual transmission, and the X5 retains the factory all-wheel-drive system. Stitching it all together was easier said than done: The development process took over a year. The engine exhales through a custom-made exhaust system, while BMW M Sport brakes and a recalibrated suspension should allow the driver to make the most of the extra power.


Specs haven’t been released, but the stock figures are telling. The most powerful E53-generation X5 was the 4.8is trim, which was built from 2004 to 2006 with a 4.8-liter V-8 rated at 355 horsepower and 360 pound-feet of torque. For context, the E60-gen M5 delivered 500 horsepower and 384 pound-feet of torque from the S85 V-10. Fieg’s restomod can give a first-generation Porsche Cayenne Turbo a run for its money, and it could have been built this way from the factory in an alternate universe: The original X5 retired after the 2006 model year, while the E60 M5 made its debut for 2006. The two cars overlapped for a single model year.


Fieg’s BMW X5 V-10 will remain a one-off, so don’t expect to find a turn-key S85 conversion kit show up in the BMW M parts catalog. At least now we know that dropping a V-10 in an X5 is possible if you have enough time, money, and fabrication skills.
